rv.q: You Can’t Take It With You is that rare show that manages to be both genuinely funny and truly heartwarming, without much recourse to the saccharine or soppy.
It’s the way we all like to remember our own crazy families, when enough time has passed to turn what might have once been painful into funny, affectionate anecdotes.

The deluxe revival is directed with unflagging energy and an assured grasp of the play's shifting rhythms by comedy pro Scott Ellis. This is a work that champions the individualist, and the director follows suit by marshaling his impeccable cast to create loopy characterizations. This is a well-oile...

What makes this revival so appealing is that Mr. Kaufman and Ms. Hart's comedy about an endearingly eccentric family has been staged by Scott Ellis with the kind of warmhearted affection that brings out the best in both the script and the cast.

There's no avoiding its old-fashionedness; You Can't Take It With You has a principal cast of 15, three acts, and a taste for whimsy over realism. Its idea of an au courant namedrop is Trotsky. OK, some of the busy business in director Scott Ellis' extravagantly good-natured production can be cloying, maybe a bit annoying.
The sprawling cast, the concise wit and the bighearted sentiment mixed with gimlet-eyed satire—playwrights haven’t topped it for decades.
A sweet revival opened Sunday at the Longacre Theatre with a perfectly picked cast but offering little reason why this old chestnut needs to be seen again.
So misguided is this production that you may find yourself sympathizing with Mr. Kirby when he calls them all insane — before falling under their spell, as inevitably he must.

Toplined by the great James Earl Jones and Rose Byrne, a perfectly swell cast can’t convince us that they’re having fun living the life of social parasites.

As Alice’s mother Penny, Kristine Nielsen who has made a career of playing daffy mothers, sisters, and aunts, gives her expected brilliant turn, adding just the right inflection or gesture to accentuate Penny’s goofy observations. She even manages to make uttering the word "potato" hilarious.
Picking a favorite in this cast is like trying to hit a moving target.
Together, Ashford and Brill are pitch-perfect as the family’s nutty live-in couple, with Ashford’s physicality alone stopping the show on multiple occasions.
Thanks to Ellis' deft hand and his first-rate cast, what audiences are guaranteed to take with them when exiting is the kind of complete and total happiness that borders on euphoria.
You Can’t Take It With You is chicken soup for the heart, the soul and all the bits in between.
Happiness, this solid production insists, is far more important than money—that’s a position that easily resonates with audiences, and it’s a message that never gets old.

Scott Ellis’ zippy and giddy revival — which sports a top quality cast including James Earl Jones, Rose Byrne, Elizabeth Ashley, Kristine Nielsen, Julie Halston, Mark Linn Baker and Annaleigh Ashford all letting loose — has a comfort food, feel good flavor to it.
It‘s occasionally a cute and quirky play, but never a great play.

cn.t: This warmhearted revival of the Depression-era classic charms with its first-rate ensemble cast and spirited staging, though some critics find the 1936 comedy feels dated and overly cloying for modern audiences.

sg.ra: Longacre's proscenium is narrow (35ft wide, 34'10" high) and the house is shallow, so Row D sits very close without neck-craning; Center Orchestra rows D-L fall inside the mezzanine overhang line (which starts around Row H) but the overhang is shallow enough that top-of-stage cut-off is not reported here, unlike deeper houses.

Longacre is a small-to-mid house (1,077 seats) so 'rear' orchestra is still close by Broadway standards; rows L-N sit behind the mezzanine overhang line (starts ~H) which trims a small slice of upper stage but preserves intimacy and drops the price noticeably versus premium D-K.

Longacre's mezzanine is 'not too high' per SeatPlan - the overhang from the balcony only starts at Row B, so Row A gets a clean head-on elevated view, and unusually generous front-row legroom is a Longacre-specific quirk called out on BroadwayWorld.

Rows D-E sit under the balcony overhang (starts Row B) but Longacre's balcony is small (249 seats, 7 rows) so the overhang depth is modest; sources consistently flag D-E as the honest middle-ground for elevated sightlines before rows F-J start feeling far from the stage.

Longacre's mezzanine rake flattens toward the back per SeatPlan ('the rake may also be slightly too shallow if a taller patron is sitting in front'), and rows F-J are explicitly called out as 'problematic' and 'not the best on account of their considerable distance from the stage' - the small house becomes a disadvantage here since the balcony takes over the better upper-level views.

Longacre-specific quirk: the front balcony rail sits high enough that multiple TripAdvisor reviewers at 5'5" and 5'7" had to lean over the bar the whole show (Macbeth 2022, Swept Away-era 2025), so Row B beats Row A for most patrons - the opposite of the usual 'front row is always best' advice. Also avoid the four structural pillars between rows B and C on the center aisles.

sg.ra: Longacre's balcony is the oldest-school part of the house - a 1913 Henry B. Herts design with four structural pillars between B-C and a steep rake that gets sound-dead at the back; SeatPlan explicitly warns 'sound quality may be inferior toward the rear' and rows D-G compound distance + pillar risk + tight legroom.
